newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Publisher Wolters takes long-term view.
newsitem.headline: Publisher Wolters takes long-term view.

text.p: Publisher Wolters Kluwer NV said on Monday it took a long-term view of its business and preferred to invest in its future rather than give investors a little more profit growth than they had already been promised.
Wolters Kluwer -- active in legal, tax, business, medical and science publishing -- has consistently outperformed the rest of the market on the Amsterdam stock exchange in recent years.
It was recently ranked among the most profitable companies in the Financial Times Global 500 where it was also ranked as one of the world's 10 biggest media companies by market value.

Wolters has delivered double-digit earnings growth year in, year out, with the exception of last year when it slowed to six percent as a result of accounting policy changes linked to its $1.9 billion acquisition of U.S. tax publisher CCH.
But it has pledged to return to annual growth of earnings per share of at least 15 percent from 1997.

Executive board chairman Cor Brakel said on Monday that the company realised by the fourth quarter of 1996 that it could have achieved several more percentage points of profit growth than the five percent it had officially forecast.
But management had decided instead to invest more in the development of electronic publishing and adding historical depth to its databases as this would bring greater long-term benefits.
"We prefer to invest more in our future than to show more profits in our books for shareholders. It's as simple as that..." he told a group of reporters.

Part of this extra investment had gone into setting up a joint venture on-line information service for doctors in the U.S. known as MD Consult in which Wolters' Lippincott-Raven Unit is collaborating with publishers WB Saunders and Mosby Yearbook.
Wolters expects electronic publishing to account for 30 percent of total annual sales by the end of the century, compared with 19 percent in 1996 and seven percent in 1995.
Brakel said he also expected investors to take a long-term view of Wolters Kluwer.
"We say to the shareholders, you should buy Wolters Kluwer because you can count on consistent profit growth and, hopefully, consistent growth of the share price," he said.
For this reason Wolters Kluwer was in no rush to join the recent fad in the Netherlands for share-splits, he said, though he did not rule out such a move in the future.
"I've always said to myself if (the share price) goes through 300 (guilders) then we should have another look at it."

Brakel said he believed that North America could be generating some 40 percent of Wolters Kluwer's sales and profits within a few years compared with some 30 percent now, due largely to the catalytic effect of the CCH buy.
CCH has also helped the Dutch company extend its geographic reach into the potentially lucrative Asia/Pacific region.
Brakel said that by improving Wolters Kluwer's contacts in that region, CCH had facilitated the late 1996 acquisition of New Zealand based ADIS, a specialised pharmacology publisher.
The Dutch company was keen to expand in Asia/Pacific, which currently contributes some three percent of revenues, and believed CCH would help it achieve this goal, he said.
